meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'house; building; home' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There's a new building on Simashko Street.

examples.text: Квартира будет отличная. На Симашко есть новый дом.
examples.trans: It'll be an excellent flat. There's a new building on Simashko Street.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'дать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to sell', paired with 'продавать'.

examples.trans: I'll sell it to the neighbour.

examples.text: Ну, как знаешь. Продам его Клавдии Викторовне.
examples.trans: Well, suit yourself. I'll sell it to Klavdia Viktorovna.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Common Russian noun meaning 'money' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The money is on the table.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very, very much', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('necessary, needed').
High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'here is; (emphasis) that's', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to find', paired with 'находить'.

examples.text: Ну где я сейчас найду грузчиков?
examples.trans: Well, where am I going to find movers right now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'bye', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Они так трогательно заботятся друг о друге.
examples.trans: They care for each other so touchingly.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'егодня').

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to remain, to be left', paired with 'оставаться'.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.
Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'арок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'present, gift' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is a present for you.

examples.text: Это семейный праздник. Как в детстве, с подарками!
examples.trans: It's a family holiday. Like when we were kids, with presents!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go, walk', paired with 'пойти'.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
examples.trans: You go to the job centre. There's work there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

examples.text: Мы сюда зачем прилетели? Я сразу сказал: с ним ничего не получится.
examples.trans: What did we even fly out here for? I said from the start: nothing will come of it with him.
Why did you even come here? Empty-handed!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'my, mine', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'something; somehow', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'хорошо'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Мы не можем его уволить. Это нехорошо.
examples.trans: We can't fire him. It's not nice.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'head' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Mum will tear my head off.

examples.text: Какая тебе опергруппа? Мне твоя мать голову оторвёт.
examples.trans: What field team? Your mother will tear my head off.

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to spin, to whirl', paired with 'закружиться'.

examples.trans: The leaves are whirling in the wind.

examples.text: Алло, Люся, привет! У Лёвы голова кружится?
examples.trans: Hello, Lyusya, hi! Is Lyova's head spinning?
